source: FTC Staff Report — Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (Sept 2022)
text: The FTC staff report describes dark patterns as design practices that trick or manipulate users into making choices they would not otherwise make and that may cause harm. It groups them into four themes: design elements that induce false beliefs, that hide or delay disclosure of material information, that lead to unauthorized charges, and that obscure or subvert privacy choices.

source: FTC Staff Report — Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (2022), Induce false beliefs
text: Examples of design elements that induce false beliefs include false claims of scarcity (low stock messages), false claims of urgency such as countdown timers that reset or that are unrelated to any real deadline, fake activity messages and fabricated social proof such as fake reviews or 'X people are viewing this' notices. The FTC Act prohibits such deceptive claims.

source: FTC Staff Report — Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (2022), Hide or delay material information
text: Design elements that hide or delay disclosure of material information include drip pricing, where mandatory fees are revealed only after the consumer has started the purchase process, and burying key terms in fine print, behind hyperlinks or in low-contrast text. Material information must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, before the consumer commits.

source: FTC Staff Report — Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (2022), Unauthorized charges
text: Design elements that lead to unauthorized charges include sneaking items into the basket, pre-checked boxes that add paid products, free trials that silently convert into paid subscriptions, and making cancellation difficult through multi-step flows, repeated retention offers or requiring the consumer to call. Consumers must give express informed consent before being charged.

source: FTC Staff Report — Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (2022), Obscure or subvert privacy choices
text: Design elements that subvert privacy choices include defaulting users into data sharing, making the privacy-protective option harder to find or less visually prominent than the option that shares more data ('accept all' bright, 'reject' hidden), confusing toggles and double-negative wording, and requiring repeated steps to decline. Choices should be presented neutrally and symmetrically.

source: FTC Act, Section 5 (15 U.S.C. § 45)
text: Section 5 of the FTC Act declares unlawful unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. A practice is deceptive if a representation, omission or practice is likely to mislead a consumer acting reasonably and is material. The net impression of an interface, not only its literal text, is evaluated.

source: Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA), 15 U.S.C. §§ 8401–8405
text: ROSCA prohibits charging consumers for goods or services sold online through a negative option feature unless the seller (1) clearly and conspicuously discloses all material terms before obtaining billing information, (2) obtains the consumer's express informed consent before charging, and (3) provides simple mechanisms for the consumer to stop recurring charges.

source: FTC Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Negative Option Marketing (Oct 2021)
text: The FTC's policy statement says negative option sellers should disclose material terms clearly and conspicuously, obtain unambiguous affirmative consent, and provide cancellation mechanisms that are at least as easy to use as the method used to sign up. Cancellation should not require the consumer to navigate obstacles such as repeated save attempts.

source: FTC Negative Option ('Click-to-Cancel') Rule, 2024 (vacated by the U.S. 8th Circuit, July 2025)
text: The FTC's 2024 amended Negative Option Rule would have required that cancelling be as easy as signing up and limited forced save attempts. A federal appeals court vacated the rule on procedural grounds in July 2025, but ROSCA and Section 5 still apply, and the FTC continues to bring cases against hard-to-cancel subscriptions (for example its 2025 settlement with Amazon over Prime enrolment and cancellation).

source: FTC Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees, 16 CFR Part 464 (effective May 2025)
text: For live-event tickets and short-term lodging, the FTC fees rule requires businesses to display the total price, including all mandatory fees, more prominently than other pricing information, and prohibits misrepresenting the nature and purpose of fees. It targets hidden 'junk fees' and drip pricing.

source: FTC Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, 16 CFR Part 465 (2024)
text: The FTC's consumer reviews rule prohibits fake or false consumer reviews and testimonials, buying reviews, and misrepresenting social-media influence indicators. Fabricated popularity or activity signals can also be deceptive under Section 5.

source: FTC v. Epic Games (2022–2023)
text: In the Epic Games (Fortnite) matter the FTC alleged that counter-intuitive, inconsistent button configurations caused players to make unwanted purchases with a single button press, and that refunds were made hard to obtain. Epic agreed to pay $245 million in refunds — an example of design-based unauthorized charges.

source: India — CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
text: Issued under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the guidelines prohibit dark patterns on platforms offering goods or services in India and list 13 specified patterns: false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action, subscription trap, interface interference, bait and switch, drip pricing, disguised advertisement, nagging, trick question, SaaS billing and rogue malwares.

source: India — CCPA Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, Annexure 1 (paraphrased)
text: False urgency: falsely stating or implying urgency or scarcity to induce an immediate purchase. Basket sneaking: adding items, donations or charges at checkout without the user's consent. Confirm shaming: using phrases, video or audio to create fear, shame or guilt to nudge the user. Subscription trap: making cancellation impossible or complex, hiding the cancel option, or forcing payment details for a free trial. Interface interference: highlighting certain information and obscuring other relevant information to misdirect the user. Drip pricing: not revealing price elements upfront or revealing them surreptitiously. Nagging: repeated requests and interactions. Trick question: confusing or vague language to misguide the user.

source: EU Digital Services Act, Article 25 (online interface design)
text: Providers of online platforms shall not design, organise or operate their interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or otherwise materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions — for example giving more prominence to certain choices, repeatedly requesting a choice already made, or making cancellation more difficult than subscribing.

source: EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU, Article 22
text: Before the consumer is bound, the trader must seek the consumer's express consent to any extra payment beyond the main contractual obligation. Consent may not be inferred from default options, such as pre-ticked boxes, that the consumer must reject to avoid the additional payment.

source: EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC, Annex I point 7
text: Falsely stating that a product will only be available for a very limited time, or only on particular terms for a very limited time, in order to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of time to make an informed choice, is a commercial practice considered unfair in all circumstances.

source: GDPR Art. 4(11) & 7, CJEU Planet49 (C-673/17, 2019)
text: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, expressed by a clear affirmative act; it must be as easy to withdraw as to give. The CJEU held in Planet49 that a pre-ticked checkbox does not constitute valid consent to cookies.

source: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns
text: The EDPB classifies deceptive design patterns such as overloading, skipping, stirring (emotional steering), obstructing, fickle (inconsistent) interfaces and left in the dark, and explains how they may infringe GDPR principles of fairness, transparency and data protection by design.

source: California CCPA Regulations, 11 CCR § 7004 (symmetry in choice)
text: Methods for submitting privacy requests and obtaining consent must use easy-to-understand language and symmetry in choice: the path to a more privacy-protective option shall not be longer or more difficult than the path to a less protective option. Confirmshaming and pre-selected options are cited as non-compliant; agreement obtained through dark patterns is not consent.

source: W3C WCAG 2.2 — Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
text: Text should have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text). Used here as an objective, measurable yardstick for whether a disclosure or alternative option is 'clear and conspicuous'.
